title: The Great Fire of London destroyed 13,200 houses and killed very few
body: The fire began in a bakery on Pudding Lane on 2 September 1666 and burned for four days. It consumed most of the medieval city, including St Paul's Cathedral, and left around 70,000 people homeless. Fewer than ten deaths were recorded, though some surely went uncounted.
takeaway: London was rebuilt in brick and stone with wider streets, and the first fire insurance companies soon followed.
visual: a seventeenth-century city of timber houses ablaze at night, people fleeing in boats across a dark river

title: The Library of Alexandria was not lost in a single fire
body: A fire during Julius Caesar's siege in 48 BCE damaged some of its scrolls, but the library carried on for centuries. It faded through lost funding, the expulsion of its scholars in 145 BCE and wars that wrecked the city. By about 270 CE it was gone.
takeaway: Knowledge is more often lost through slow neglect than sudden disaster.
source: Roger Bagnall, Proceedings of the American Philosophical Society (2002)
visual: a grand columned hall of scroll shelves with dust and cobwebs gathering, a few scholars leaving through a distant doorway

title: In 1518 hundreds of people danced for days and could not stop
body: In July 1518 a woman began dancing in a street in Strasbourg. Within a month as many as 400 people had joined her, some until they collapsed. The city council first hired musicians, believing more dancing would cure it, and then banned music.
takeaway: Historians think it was a mass psychological illness in a population worn down by famine and disease.
source: John Waller, A Time to Dance, a Time to Die (2008)
visual: a crowd of exhausted people in sixteenth-century dress dancing wildly in a town square while onlookers stare in alarm

title: Tulip mania did not ruin the Dutch economy
body: In early 1637 the price of rare tulip bulbs in Holland soared and then collapsed within weeks. The popular story has fortunes destroyed and merchants drowning themselves. A historian who searched the archives found almost nobody bankrupted and no wider economic damage.
takeaway: The lurid version comes from pamphlets written to mock the traders, repeated in a best-selling book in 1841.
source: Anne Goldgar, Tulipmania: Money, Honor, and Knowledge in the Dutch Golden Age (2007)
visual: a single streaked red and white tulip in a vase on a table surrounded by Dutch merchants in dark coats leaning in to bid

title: An emperor's regret is carved on rocks across the subcontinent
body: After conquering Kalinga around 261 BCE, the Mauryan emperor Ashoka had messages cut into rocks and pillars from Afghanistan to Karnataka. One records his remorse at the deaths the war caused. Nobody could read them until James Prinsep deciphered the Brahmi script in 1837.
takeaway: The four-lion capital of his pillar at Sarnath is now the national emblem of India.
source: Romila Thapar, Asoka and the Decline of the Mauryas (1961)
visual: a tall polished sandstone pillar topped with four lions standing in a quiet grove, ancient script carved around its shaft

title: Farmers digging a well found an army of 8,000 clay soldiers
body: In March 1974 villagers near the Chinese city of Xi'an struck fragments of a clay figure. Archaeologists uncovered an army of about 8,000 life-size soldiers with horses and chariots, buried around 210 BCE to guard the first emperor of China, Qin Shi Huang. No two faces are alike.
takeaway: The emperor's own tomb chamber nearby has still not been opened.
source: UNESCO World Heritage Centre; Emperor Qin Shi Huang's Mausoleum Site Museum
visual: long ranks of life-size clay warriors standing in earthen trenches, each face different, lit by shafts of light

title: A stone monument is 6,000 years older than Stonehenge
body: At Göbekli Tepe in south-eastern Turkey, people raised rings of T-shaped stone pillars up to 5.5 metres tall around 9500 BCE. They carved foxes, snakes and vultures on them. Its builders were hunter-gatherers, who had neither pottery nor metal tools.
takeaway: It suggests that large gatherings and shared belief may have come before farming, not after it.
source: Klaus Schmidt, German Archaeological Institute; UNESCO World Heritage Centre
visual: a circle of massive T-shaped stone pillars carved with animals on a bare hilltop under a star-filled sky

title: India's first passenger train ran 34 km in 1853
body: On 16 April 1853 a train of 14 carriages carrying about 400 guests left Bori Bunder in Bombay for Thane, hauled by three steam locomotives named Sahib, Sindh and Sultan. The journey took about an hour and was sent off with a 21-gun salute.
takeaway: The network that grew from it now covers about 68,000 km and carries over 20 million passengers a day.
source: Indian Railways; National Rail Museum, New Delhi
visual: a steam locomotive pulling wooden carriages out of a nineteenth-century Indian station past a cheering crowd

title: The Berlin Wall opened because of a muddled press conference
body: On 9 November 1989 the East German spokesman Günter Schabowski read out new travel rules he had barely seen. Asked when they took effect, he said immediately. They were meant to begin the next day, with paperwork. Thousands went to the checkpoints, and a guard opened the gate.
takeaway: Great changes can turn on small accidents, once the pressure behind them is large enough.
source: Federal Agency for Civic Education, Germany; Mary Elise Sarotte, The Collapse (2014)
visual: a crowd pressing against a floodlit border checkpoint at night, a barrier pole lifting as guards stand aside

title: Of the 270 men who set out to sail round the world, 18 came home
body: Ferdinand Magellan left Spain in 1519 with five ships. He was killed in the Philippines in April 1521. Storms, mutiny, scurvy and starvation took most of the rest. One ship, the Victoria, reached Spain in September 1522 under Juan Sebastián Elcano.
takeaway: Magellan never completed the first circumnavigation of the globe. His crew did.
source: Antonio Pigafetta, journal of the voyage (1525); Encyclopaedia Britannica
visual: a single battered sixteenth-century sailing ship with torn sails limping into a harbour at dawn
